1:1: Κυρίου Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ τῆς ἐλπίδος ἡμῶν
Here, our hope refers to the person in whom we have hope.
1:2: Paul speaks of his close relationship to Timothy as though Timothy were his genuine child. Paul means that he is Timothy’s spiritual father, and Paul loves Timothy in the way a father loves his child.

Here, the word genuine indicates that the child is considered to be someone’s child in the full legal sense. For example, a child born to an unmarried woman would not be considered genuine. In the context of the metaphor, the word indicates that Timothy has acted as a son should act toward Paul.
After stating his name and the name of the person to whom he is writing, Paul adds a blessing for Timothy.
Father is an important title for God the Father that describes his relationship with Jesus, his Son.
1:3: Here Paul could be implying that, when he previously urged Timothy to remain in Ephesus, he was: (1) in Ephesus with Timothy and was about to leave for Macedonia; (2) already on his way to Macedonia. In this case, Paul would be referring to a letter he had previously written to Timothy.
The implication is that these people were teaching different things than what Paul and Timothy taught, not that they were teaching in a different way.
1:4: The word myths refers to a certain kind of story that is generally considered to be untrustworthy. This kind of story is often about what important people did a long time ago. Often, many people in a culture know these stories but do not consider them to be reliable historical narratives.
Paul says endless here as an overstatement for emphasis.
The word genealogies refers to lists of someone’s ancestors.
Here, the word translated arguments could refer to: (1) debates or heated discussions; (2) questions or enquiries.
Here Paul could be implying that the stewardship of God: (1) is promoted or accomplished when people have faith; (2) is known or experienced when people have faith.
1:5: Here Paul uses the word Now to introduce background information that will help Timothy understand the purpose of what he is commanding him to do.
Here, the phrase the command refers to what Paul has instructed Timothy to tell the “certain ones” in Ephesus (see 1:3–4).
In Paul’s culture, the heart is the place where humans think and feel.
A conscience that is good is one that does not convict a person of doing anything wrong.
1:6: Paul speaks as if a pure heart, good conscience, and sincere faith were a mark or target that some people have missed. Paul means that these people have failed to attain those things.

Here Paul speaks of abandoning what is good to focus on foolish talk as if it were turning away from those good things to foolish talk. He means that these people have stopped pursuing the good things that Paul mentioned in the previous verse and instead are focusing on things of little consequence.
1:7: Here, the word law refers specifically to the laws that God gave the Israelites through Moses.
μήτε ἃ λέγουσιν, μήτε περὶ τίνων διαβεβαιοῦνται
Here, the clauses what they are saying and what they insist on mean similar things. Paul is using the two clauses together for emphasis.
1:8: Here, the word law refers specifically to the laws that God gave the Israelites through Moses.
Here Paul indicates that the law {is} good when people use it as God intended it to be used, that is, lawfully.
1:9: Here, the phrase the law could refer to: (1) the laws that God gave the Israelites through Moses; (2) laws in general.

In this list Paul uses several compound words to express his meaning concisely and vividly. In each case the first term in the compound, a noun, is the object of the second term in the compound, a verb. Three of these compound words are in this verse, and two more are in the next verse.
1:10: Here, the word homosexuals refers to men who lie with or have sex with other men.
Here, the word kidnappers refers to people who kidnap others and sell them as slaves.
Here Paul speaks as if teaching could be healthy. He means that this kind of teaching is good and reliable in every way and has no defect or corruption.
1:12: Here, the phrase placing me into service could be: (1) a result from how Jesus considered him to be trustworthy; (2) a reason why Paul knows that Jesus considered him to be trustworthy; (3) a second thing that Jesus did for Paul.
1:13: Here Paul is referring specifically to his life before he believed in Jesus.
Here Paul could be implying that he blasphemed: (1) Jesus; (2) God.

Here Paul could be implying that: (1) he acted in an ignorant way while he did not have faith; (2) he acted in an ignorant way because he did not have faith; (3) he acted ignorantly and without faith.
Here Paul implies that he did not fully know or understand the things that he did before he believed.
1:14: ὑπερεπλεόνασεν … ἡ χάρις τοῦ Κυρίου ἡμῶν
Paul speaks of the grace of the Lord as if it were a liquid that filled a container until overflowed. He means that he received an extraordinary amount of grace.
Here, the phrase our Lord could refer to: (1) Jesus; (2) God the Father.
Here, the phrase in Christ Jesus could describe: (1) both faith and love; (2) just love.
Paul uses the spatial metaphor in Christ Jesus to describe the union of believers with Christ. In this case, being in Christ Jesus, or united to Christ Jesus, explains how Paul has faith and love.
1:15: Here, word represents what Paul is about to write using words.
The terms trustworthy and worthy of all acceptance mean similar things. Paul is using the two terms together for emphasis.
Here Paul speaks of the most sinful person, himself, as if he were first in a sequence.
1:16: Here Paul could be: (1) again speaking of the most sinful person, himself, as if he were first in a sequence.
1:17: Many ancient manuscripts read the only God. Other ancient manuscripts read “the only wise God.” It is likely that the people who copied these manuscripts accidentally or intentionally included the word “wise” here because of the similar phrase “the only wise God” in Romans 16:27.
The terms honor and glory mean similar things. Paul is using the two terms together for emphasis.
Here, the phrase forever {and} ever identifies an action that will never end, and it strongly emphasizes that it will never end.
1:18: Here, the phrase This command could refer to: (1) the command that Paul gave to Timothy in 1:3–5 about staying in Ephesus and what to do there; (2) the instructions later in this verse about fighting the good fight.
Paul speaks of his command as if it were an object that he could physically put in front of Timothy. He means that he has given this command to Timothy.
Paul speaks of his close relationship to Timothy as though Timothy were his child. Paul means that he is Timothy’s spiritual father, and Paul loves Timothy in the way a father loves his child.

Here Paul implies that some people had given prophecies about Timothy sometime earlier. These prophecies may have been spoken before Timothy was born, before Timothy became a believer, or when Timothy officially joined Paul to proclaim the gospel. If possible, leave the exact timing of the prophecies unstated, as Paul does.

Here, the phrase in them could indicate that Timothy should fight the good fight: (1) as the prophecies indicated that he would; (2) by means of the prophecies, which function like weapons in the fight; (3) with the prophecies as his motivation.
Paul speaks about Timothy serving God by preaching the gospel and by confronting false teachers as if he were fighting a good fight.
Here, the phrase the good fight could indicate: (1) that someone is fighting well; (2) that the fight is right or just.
1:19: A conscience that is good is one that does not convict a person of doing anything wrong.
Here Paul refers to how ships that sailed on the ocean could break apart or sink. When this happened, people had to try to survive in the water or swim to shore.

Paul speaks of these people and their faith as if they were on a ship that had sunk. He means that these people have lost their faith, just as people in a shipwreck lose the ship and everything on it.
1:20: The words Hymenaeus and Alexander are the names of two men.

To give someone over to someone else refers to transferring a person from one authority to another. Here, then, Paul says that he has transferred these two men from under the authority of the church to under the authority of Satan.
2:1: Here Paul could be using the word first: (1) to indicate that what he is about to urge is the most important thing he will urge; (2) to indicate that what he is about to urge is the first of several commands he will give.

Here Paul uses four words that refer to four types of prayer. The word prayers is the most general, and the word thanksgivings refers to thanking God for something rather than asking for something. The words requests and intercessions both refer to asking God to do something, and they mean very similar things. Paul uses these four words to indicate that believers should be praying for all men in many different ways.
2:2: The terms peaceful and quiet mean similar things. Paul is using the two terms together for emphasis.
2:3: καλὸν καὶ ἀπόδεκτον ἐνώπιον τοῦ Σωτῆρος ἡμῶν, Θεοῦ
Here, the phrase before God our Savior could go with: (1) just acceptable; (2) both good and acceptable.
The terms good and acceptable mean similar things. Paul is using the two terms together for emphasis.
Here, the phrase before God refers to God’s evaluation or view about something.
2:4: Paul speaks of knowledge of the truth as if it were a place where people could come. He means that God desires that all people gain knowledge of the truth.
2:5: Here Paul uses the word man to emphasize that Christ Jesus is human, just like the men for whom he functions as a mediator.
2:6: Here, the phrase having given himself implies that Jesus died willingly.

Here Paul speaks as if Jesus were a price or ransom he himself gave to free all from someone or something that owned or controlled them. He means that Jesus obtained forgiveness for his people’s sins and keeps those sins from controlling them. This is an important biblical image, so if possible preserve the figure of speech or express the idea in simile form.
Here, the word testimony could refer to: (1) people giving testimony about what Jesus did; (2) what Jesus did, giving testimony to how God wants to save all people.

Here, the phrase translated in its own times indicates that something happens at an appropriate time or period of time. More specifically, the times could be appropriate because: (1) they fit with the testimony; (2) God chose them.
2:7: A herald is someone who is sent out to announce a message.
ἀλήθειαν λέγω ἐν Χριστῷ, οὐ ψεύδομαι
These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea in negative form.
Here Paul uses the spatial metaphor in Christ to describe his union with Christ. In this case, Paul claims that he is speaking the truth as surely as he is in Christ, or united to Christ.
Many ancient manuscripts read in Christ. Other ancient manuscripts do not include these words.
Here, the phrase in faith and truth could provide: (1) the content of what Paul teaches; (2) the manner in which Paul teaches.

Here, the phrase faith and truth could: (1) refer to two distinct things that Paul teaches; (2) express a single idea by using two words connected with and. The word truth tells what the faith is like.
2:8: Here Paul implies that every place is any location where the believers are worshiping God.
In Paul’s culture, lifting up one’s hands was a common posture for someone who was praying.
Paul describes as holy one part of the person, the hands, to indicate that the entire person is to be holy.
Here, the word translated argument could be describing: (1) quarrels or conflicts; (2) doubts.
2:9: Here Paul gives examples of specific types of hairstyles, jewelry, and clothing that, in his culture, could have indicated that a woman was showing off her wealth, power, or beauty.

In Paul’s culture, women used many different kinds of hairstyles. People considered some of them to be more elaborate and ostentatious than others. Paul implies with the word braids that he is referring to a hairstyle that people would consider to be elaborate or ostentatious.
Here Paul is referring to ornaments or jewelry made out of gold.
The word pearls refers to beautiful and valuable mineral balls that people use as jewelry.
2:10: ὃ πρέπει γυναιξὶν ἐπαγγελλομέναις θεοσέβειαν, δι’ ἔργων ἀγαθῶν

Here Paul implies that the women should “adorn themselves” through good works. He speaks of these good works as if they were articles of clothing in order to indicate that it should be good works that characterize these women, just as clothing characterizes people.
2:11: Here, the word translated woman could refer: (1) generally to any female believer; (2) specifically to any woman who is married. This is indicated by the switch from the plural “women” in the previous verses to the singular “woman” here.

Here, the word translated quietness could describe: (1) learning unobtrusively and peacefully. Paul used a similar word (“quiet”) in 2:2, where it described a life that is calm and peaceful; (2) learning without speaking.
Here Paul does not state to whom or what the women are to be in all submission. If possible, you also should not express to whom or what they are to be in all submission.
2:12: Here, just as in 2:11, the word translated woman could refer: (1) generally to any female believer. In this case, the word man refers generally to any male believer; (2) specifically to any woman who is married. This is indicated by the switch from the plural “women” in 2:9–10 to the singular “woman” in 2:11 and here. In this case, the word man refers to the wife’s husband.
Here Paul could be implying that women are not permitted to teach: (1) men; (2) anyone during a public meeting of believers.
Here, the word translated to have authority over could refer to: (1) any kind of rule or leadership; (2) dominating or exercising abusive authority.

Here, just as in 2:11, the word translated quietness could describe: (1) being unobtrusive and peaceful. Paul used a similar word (“quiet”) in 2:2, where it described a life that is calm and peaceful; (2) not speaking.
2:13: Here Paul refers to a story found in Genesis 2:5–25. In this story, when God made the first humans, he created a man named Adam. After that, he created a woman named Eve.
2:14: Here Paul refers to a story found in Genesis 3:1–7. In this story, a talking serpent approaches Eve and convinces her to eat fruit that God had commanded her and Adam not to eat. She ate some of it, and then she gave some to Adam, and he also ate some of it.
Here Paul speaks as if transgression were a location that Eve came into. He means that she committed a transgression.
2:15: Christians debate the meaning of this clause. For some of the possible interpretations, see the chapter introduction. The two most likely interpretations are that: (1) she (Eve or women in general) will be saved by God, who will use childbearing as the means by which he sends the Messiah into the world. In this case, childbearing describes one means by which God accomplishes salvation; (2) she (women in general) will be saved spiritually as they have children and act as mothers. In this case, childbearing describes the circumstances in which the women will be saved.

Here, the phrase with self-control could provide: (1) the fourth and last item in the list; (2) the manner in which the women should remain in faith and love and holiness; (3) the manner in which the women should remain in holiness.
3:1: Here, just as in 1:15, word represents what Paul writes by using words.
3:2: The terms temperate and self-controlled mean similar things. Paul is using the two terms together for emphasis.
3:3: Many ancient manuscripts read not a brawler.
3:4: Here, the phrase with all dignity could describe: (1) another characteristic of the children; (2) another way the children treat their parent, the overseer; (3) how the overseer should treat his children.
3:5: Here Paul uses an imaginary situation to show that people who do not lead their own households well are not able to lead the church well.
Paul is using the question form to strongly deny that this kind of person can take care of the church of God.
Here Paul refers to the specific church whom the person would be taking care of.
3:6: ἵνα μὴ … εἰς κρίμα ἐμπέσῃ τοῦ διαβόλου
Here Paul refers to experiencing judgment as if it were falling into a hole.
Here Paul speaks of becoming prideful as if it were being puffed up by air.
Here Paul implies that a new convert might be puffed up, or prideful, because of being made an overseer so quickly.
3:7: The phrase the ones outside identifies people who do not belong to the group of believers.
Here Paul refers to experiencing reproach as if it were falling into a hole.
Here Paul speaks of how the devil gains power or control over people as if he were trapping.
3:8: Here Paul refers to people who change what they say to match the situation as if they were double-talkers, or people who say two words at the same time.
Here, the word translated as greedy could refer to: (1) strong desire for more money and goods than one needs; (2) gaining money and goods by shameful means.
3:9: ἔχοντας τὸ μυστήριον τῆς πίστεως ἐν καθαρᾷ συνειδήσει
Here, the phrase with a pure conscience could describe: (1) these people’s lives in general; (2) the manner in which these people have the mystery.
Here, the word having implies that these people are faithful to and continue to believe what they are having.
A conscience that is pure is one that does not convict a person of doing anything wrong.
3:10: Here, the phrase being blameless could give: (1) the condition that must be fulfilled for them to serve; (2) a description of the people who can serve.
3:11: Here, the word translated women could refer to: (1) female deacons; (2) the wives of deacons.
3:12: After speaking about “women” in the previous verse, Paul could be using the word deacons to refer to: (1) male deacons; (2) all deacons.

The phrase children and their own households is not making a distinction between children and households by indicating that the children are not part of the household. Rather, the phrase emphasizes that the children are a particularly important part of the households.
3:13: Here, the phrase the ones having served could refer: (1) just to the deacons, whom Paul has discussed in 3:8–12; (2) both to the deacons and to the overseers, whom he has discussed in 3:1–12.

Here Paul speaks as if these people will have good standing. He could be indicating that they will gain: (1) respect and influence among believers; (2) a specific position or office that is respected.
Here, the phrase much confidence in the faith could mean that these people: (1) will have much confidence in their faith; (2) will speak with much confidence about the faith.
Here, the phrase the faith {that is} in Christ Jesus could refer to: (1) the act of having faith in Christ Jesus; (2) what people believe about Christ Jesus when they have faith in him.
3:14: Here, the phrase these things could refer to: (1) everything that Paul has included in the letter; (2) what Paul has written in the letter so far.
3:15: Here Paul may be implying that: (1) he himself might choose to delay; (2) something might cause or force Paul to delay.
Here Paul could be implying that he is instructing Timothy in how: (1) believers should behave; (2) Timothy should behave.
Here Paul speaks of believers as if they were part of the household of God. He means that God considers them to be members of his own family.

Here Paul speaks as if the truth were the roof of a building and of the church as if it were a pillar and support that held up that roof. He means that the church helps to preserve and proclaim the truth.
The terms pillar and support mean similar things. Paul is using the two terms together for emphasis.
3:16: Here, the word flesh refers to human existence in its weakness and frailty. Paul means that Jesus was human.
Here, the phrase was justified could indicate that Jesus was: (1) proved by the Holy Spirit to be who he said he was; (2) declared innocent by the Holy Spirit.
Here, the word nations could refer to: (1) non-Jewish people; (2) all groups of people.
Here, the phrase in the world indicates that people in many places throughout the world believed in Jesus.
Here Paul implies that Jesus was taken up into heaven.
Here, the phrase in glory could describe: (1) how Jesus was taken up; (2) Jesus, as he was taken up.
4:1: Here, the phrase later times could refer to: (1) the last days in general, the period between Jesus’ resurrection and second coming; (2) sometime later than when the Spirit spoke.
Here Paul speaks of rejecting or failing to persist in the faith as if it were falling away from a location where the faith was.
Here, the word faith could refer to: (1) the act of having faith in Jesus; (2) what people believe about Jesus when they have faith in him.
Here, the phrase paying attention to could introduce: (1) a further description of what these people do; (2) the reason why these people fall away; (3) the means by which these people fall away.
Here, the phrase deceiving spirits refers to evil spiritual beings who deceive people.
4:2: Here, the word in could introduce: (1) the means or cause by which some people will pay attention to deceiving spirits and teachings of demons; (2) the means by which they learn the teachings of demons.

Here Paul could be speaking as if these people’s conscience: (1) had been seared, so that it can no longer feel anything. In this case, he means that they no longer feel convicted about what is right and wrong; (2) had been branded and thus marked either as belonging to Satan or as a sinner.
4:3: Here Paul implies that the false teachers were telling people to abstain from certain kinds of foods. They were not telling people to abstain from eating in general.
4:5: Here, word represents something God has communicated using words.
Here Paul implies that this prayer contains the thanksgiving he referred to in 4:4.
4:6: Here Paul speaks of his instructions as if they were objects that Timothy would place before other people. He means that Timothy will speak his instructions to these people.
Paul is using the term brothers to mean people who share the same faith.
Here, the phrase being nourished could introduce: (1) a description of a good servant; (2) another condition for being a good servant; (3) the result of being a good servant.
Here Paul speaks as if the words of the faith and of the good teaching were food that nourished Timothy. He means that these words train Timothy and make him stronger spiritually.
4:7: The term old-womanish describes something that is silly or foolish. Paul does not mean that these myths always came from older women or that older women were more likely to believe the myths.

The word myths refers to a certain kind of story that is generally considered to be untrustworthy. This kind of story is often about what important people did a long time ago. Often, many people in a culture know these stories but do not consider them to be reliable historical narratives.
Here Paul speaks as if Timothy were an athlete who needed to train himself. He means that Timothy needs to work hard, as an athlete does, in order to become godly.
4:8: Here, the phrase having promise introduces something about godliness that supports the claim that godliness is useful for all.
ζωῆς τῆς νῦν, καὶ τῆς μελλούσης
Here Paul is referring to true life with God that people can have now and in the coming future, when God resurrects people after they have died.
4:9: πιστὸς ὁ λόγος, καὶ πάσης ἀποδοχῆς ἄξιος
This verse is identical to the first clause in 1:15.
Here, the phrase The word could refer: (1) ahead to what Paul is about to write in 4:10; (2) back to what Paul wrote in 4:8.
4:10: The terms toil and struggle mean similar things. Paul is using the two terms together for emphasis.
Here Paul could mean that God is the Savior of believers: (1) in a special way compared to how he saves all men; (2) in reality, compared to how he is the only potential Savior for all men.
4:12: Here Paul implies that people might despise Timothy because of his youth.
Here, word represents things that Timothy speaks using words.
4:13: πρόσεχε τῇ ἀναγνώσει, τῇ παρακλήσει, τῇ διδασκαλίᾳ
Here Paul implies that the reading, exhortation, and teaching take place in public meetings of the church where Timothy was.
4:14: Paul speaks of Timothy as if he were a container that could hold God’s gift. He means that Timothy has this gift.
Here Paul implies that this gift is a specific ability or skill that God had given Timothy for his ministry.
μετὰ ἐπιθέσεως τῶν χειρῶν τοῦ πρεσβυτερίου
Here Paul is speaking of a ceremony during which the church leaders put their hands on Timothy. When they did that, they were commissioning Timothy to go with Paul and proclaim the gospel.
4:15: Here Paul speaks as if Timothy could physically be inside the instructions he has given to Timothy. He means that Timothy always needs to focus on and perform these things.

Here Paul implies that Timothy’s progress will be in his Christian life and ministry. In other words, he will have progress as he believes in Jesus, learns more about the gospel, and serves others using his gift.
5:1: Paul wants Timothy to exhort each older man as he would speak to his own father, and he wants Timothy to exhort younger men as he would speak to his own younger brothers. He means that Timothy should speak to these people as if they filled the roles of father and brothers in his own family.
Here Paul could be implying that these men are younger than: (1) Timothy; (2) the older men. In this case, Paul is using the word younger to refer to a general category.
5:2: Here Paul could be implying that these women are older or younger: (1) than Timothy; (2) in general terms. In this case, Paul is using the words older and younger to refer to general categories.

Paul wants Timothy to exhort older women as he would speak to his own mother, and he wants Timothy to exhort younger women as he would speak to his own younger sisters. He means that Timothy should speak to these people as if they filled the roles of mother and sisters in his own family.

Here, the phrase in all purity could describe: (1) only how Timothy should exhort younger women. In this case, Paul is especially concerned about sexual purity; (2) how Timothy should exhort older and younger men and older and younger women. In this case, Paul is speaking about purity in general.
5:3: Here Paul implies that one of the ways to Honor widows is to provide for their needs.
Here Paul defines which category of widows he is particularly referring to. The word real indicates that these women are not only widows but also have no close relatives to support them.
5:4: Here Paul implies that these children and grandchildren are adults who are able to care for others.
Here, the word first indicates that doing what Paul commands in this verse is very important.
Here, learn represents experiencing something by doing it repeatedly.
Here Paul implies that one important way to treat one’s family in a godly way is to take care of and provide for them.

Here Paul speaks as if people taking care of their forebears were a repayment for how their forebears took care of them. He means that this is an appropriate way for people to treat their forebears given what the forebears did for them.
Here, the phrase before God refers to God’s evaluation or view about something.
5:5: The two phrases real widow and one having been left alone express a single idea. The phrase one having been left alone explains what it means to be a real widow.

Here Paul again defines what kind of widow he is particularly referring to. As in 5:3, the word real indicates that these women are not only widows but also have no close relatives to support them. The phrase having been left alone similarly indicates that this kind of widow has no close relatives.
προσμένει ταῖς δεήσεσιν καὶ ταῖς προσευχαῖς
Here Paul speaks as if requests and prayers were a location that a widow remains in. He means that this widow frequently and persistently makes requests and prayers to God.
The terms requests and prayers mean similar things. Paul is using the two terms together for emphasis.
Here, the phrase night and day indicates that this widow prays during both the day and the night. This means that she was praying very often every day.
5:6: Here Paul describes widows who act like this as if they had died even though they are living. He means that they are like dead people because they are spiritually dead.
5:7: Here, the phrase these things refers to the instructions about widows and their families in the preceding verses (see 5:4–6). Paul includes the word also because he earlier told Timothy to “command” other things (see 4:11).
5:8: Here, the phrase household members refers specifically to one’s close family, the family members who live together in one house.
Here, the word faith could refer to: (1) the act of having faith in Jesus; (2) what people believe about Jesus when they have faith in him.
Here Paul implies that this person is a worse sinner than an unbeliever, since unbelievers generally do take care of their families.
5:9: Here Paul implies that the church had a list of widows who truly needed the church to support them. In this and the following verse, Paul gives a list of qualifications for which widows could be put on this list.
5:10: Here the clauses that begin with if could be: (1) examples of good works that the widow should have done; (2) separate requirements for being enrolled as a widow in need of support.

In this culture, people walked barefoot or in sandals on roads that were dusty or muddy. When they arrived at a house, usually they or a servant would wash their feet to clean off the dust or mud. Washing off someone’s feet was generally considered a menial or lowly task.
Here Paul may be referring to washing feet in order to: (1) give another specific example of the good works that this widow has done; (2) describe more generally any kind of humble service.
Here, Paul speaks as if every good work were a person whom this widow followed. He means that she has worked hard always to do every good work.
Paul says every here as an overstatement for emphasis.
5:11: Here Paul implies that Timothy should refuse to enroll the younger widows on the list of widows whom the church would support (see 5:9).

Here, the phrase indulge themselves against Christ could mean that these widows: (1) desire to live self-indulgently in contrast to obeying Christ; (2) desiring to have sex in contrast to serving Christ as widows.

Since in 5:14 Paul recommends that these widows marry again, here he must have a specific situation in mind where wanting to marry is wrong. He could be implying that these widows want to marry: (1) anyone who has money and can support their self-indulgent lifestyles, even if that person is an unbeliever; (2) after they have promised to serve in the church as widows without marrying again.
5:12: Here, the word faith could refer to: (1) the faith that the younger widows had in Jesus. In this case, they have annulled this faith by marrying anyone, even an unbeliever, so that they can indulge their selfish desires; (2) a commitment that the widows made that they would remain as widows and serve the Christian community for the rest of their lives. In this case, they have annulled this commitment by choosing to marry when they said that they would not marry.
Here, the word first refers to faith that the widows had before they wanted to get married.
5:13: Here, learn represents experiencing something by doing it repeatedly.
Here Paul implies that these young widows may visit one house after another. The rest of the verse implies that they would do this in order to gossip and learn what other people were doing.
φλύαροι καὶ περίεργοι, λαλοῦσαι τὰ μὴ δέοντα

These two terms and a phrase mean similar things. The word babblers refers to people who say many things that do not mean very much. The word meddlers refers to people who try to figure out what others are doing and interfere in it. The phrase saying what they should not refers to speaking about things that should not be spoken about. Paul is using these three terms together for emphasis.
5:14: Here Paul is referring to the younger widows whom he has been speaking about in 5:11–13.
Here, the reviling could be directed toward: (1) believers in general; (2) just the widows.
Here, the phrase the one opposing could refer to: (1) Satan. In this case, Satan probably would use other people to revile believers; (2) any person who opposes or attacks believers.
5:15: Here Paul speaks of abandoning what God wants believers to do and instead focusing on what Satan wants them to do as if they were turning away after Satan. He means that these people have stopped doing what God wants and are instead doing what Satan wants.
5:16: The implication is that she has widows within her extended family.
Paul speaks of the church having to help more widows than it is able to help as if it were carrying too much weight on its back.

Here Paul again defines the kind of widow to which he is particularly referring. As in 5:3, the word real indicates that these women are not only widows but also have no close relatives to support them.
5:17: Here, the phrase double honor could refer to: (1) two different kinds of honor, respect and payment; (2) a large amount of honor; (3) double the honor or payment given to other people whom the church supported.
Here, word represents what these elders preach using words.
5:18: Here, Paul speaks of the Scripture as if it were a person who could say something. He means that these words can be read in the Scripture.
When he quotes this passage, Paul is implying that the leaders of the church are like an ox that is threshing. Both are doing work and both deserve to be supported as they do that work.

In Paul’s culture, farmers often would make oxen thresh, that is, walk on harvested wheat to separate the kernels of grain from the wheat stalks. Some people would muzzle an ox while it was threshing in order to keep the ox from eating the grain. The point of the command is that the ox should be allowed to eat what it is working to produce: the grain.
5:20: Here, the phrase The ones sinning could refer to: (1) elders who have sinned; (2) believers who have sinned.
Here Paul implies that these people will have fear of sinning.
5:21: Here Paul could be: (1) indicating that God and Christ Jesus and the chosen angels know and approve what Paul has written; (2) putting Timothy under oath, making him swear by God and Christ Jesus and the chosen angels, that he will do what Paul has written.
Here, the phrase these things refers to the instructions that Paul has given to Timothy about how to treat elders (see 5:17–20).
χωρὶς προκρίματος, μηδὲν ποιῶν κατὰ πρόσκλισιν
The terms prejudgment and partiality mean similar things. Paul is using the two terms together for emphasis.
5:22: Here Paul is speaking of a ceremony during which church leaders would Place their hands on a person. When they did that, they were commissioning that person to serve God in a specific way, usually as a leader.
Here, Paul implies that Timothy might share in the sins of others if he helps to appoint leaders who are sinning or if he does not confront leaders who are sinning.
5:23: Here Paul means that Timothy should have a little wine in addition to the water he was drinking. In Paul’s culture, people believed that wine could help with certain physical problems and illnesses.
5:24: προάγουσαι εἰς κρίσιν, τισὶν δὲ καὶ ἐπακολουθοῦσιν

Here Paul speaks of sins as if they were people who could be going ahead of or who could follow those who sinned into the place where judgment happens. He means that everyone knows that some people are guilty before they experience judgment, but with other people no one knows that they are guilty before they experience judgment.
Here, the word judgment could refer to: (1) how God will judge everyone when Jesus comes back; (2) how the church or its leaders will judge people who are sinning.
5:25: καὶ τὰ ἔργα τὰ καλὰ πρόδηλα
Here Paul implies that these are the good works of some people, since he states in the second half of the verse that some good works are not evident.
Here Paul is referring to good works that are otherwise because they are not immediately evident.
6:1: Here Paul speaks of people who work as slaves as though they were working animals with a yoke around their necks. He could mean: (1) that these people truly are slaves and not just workers or servants; (2) that these slaves work for cruel or strict masters.
Here, name represents a person, especially that person’s reputation and nature.
6:2: Paul is using the term brothers to mean people who share the same faith.

Here, the word translated rather could: (1) introduce what the slaves should do instead of despising their masters; (2) indicate that slaves should serve believing masters even better than they might serve unbelieving masters.

Here Paul could be indicating that: (1) the masters receive benefaction from the slaves. Since benefaction was usually something that someone with money and resources gave to someone without those things, Paul is indicating that believing slaves can actually function as benefactors for their believing masters; (2) the masters give benefaction to their slaves; (3) the masters and slaves together give benefaction to others.
6:3: The implication is that some people were teaching different things than what Paul and Timothy taught, not that they were teaching in a different way.
μὴ προσέρχεται ὑγιαίνουσι λόγοις … τῇ … διδασκαλίᾳ
Here Paul speaks of someone agreeing with words and teaching as if that person were coming to those words and teaching.
Here Paul speaks as if words could be healthy. He means that these words are good and reliable in every way and have no defect or corruption.
Here, words represents things spoken using words.
6:4: Here Paul speaks of becoming prideful as if it were being puffed up by air.
Paul says nothing here as an overstatement for emphasis.

Here Paul speaks as if these false teachers were sick and as if their illnesses were controversies and word battles. He means that they are constantly participating in these controversies and word battles, but those things are bad for them.
Here Paul refers to arguments about what words mean as if they were battles.
Here, the word evil could indicate that the suspicions: (1) themselves are evil; (2) are that others have done what is evil.
6:5: Here, Paul speaks of frequent quarrels and arguments between people as if they were constant friction.
Many ancient manuscripts end this verse with the phrase a means of gain.
6:6: Here, the word gain is the same word that Paul used in 6:5 for gaining money. Here, he uses the word to refer to gaining something else, which he does not state explicitly. He could be referring to salvation, spiritual blessings, or something else.
6:7: Here Paul is referring to when a person is born. At birth, a person does not own anything or contribute anything to the world.
Here Paul is referring to when a person dies. At death, a person no longer owns anything or contributes anything to the world.
6:8: Here, the word covering could refer to: (1) clothing primarily; (2) any kind of protection from the elements, whether clothing, house, or shelter.
6:9: Here Paul speaks as if temptation and a trap and many foolish and harmful desires were holes that people could fall into. He means that these people will experience these things and be unable to escape from them.
Here Paul speaks of how these people are not free to do whatever they want as if they had fallen into a trap.
αἵτινες βυθίζουσι τοὺς ἀνθρώπους εἰς ὄλεθρον καὶ ἀπώλειαν
Here Paul speaks as if these people’s desires would sink or drown them in ruin and destruction. He means that these desires will lead to complete ruin and destruction.
The terms ruin and destruction mean similar things. Paul is using the two terms together for emphasis.
6:10: ῥίζα … πάντων τῶν κακῶν ἐστιν ἡ φιλαργυρία
Paul speaks of evil as if it were a plant, and of the love of money as if it were the root from which that plant grew. He means that the love of money leads to all the evils.
Paul says all here as an overstatement for emphasis.
Paul speaks of desiring money as if it were an evil guide that intentionally leads people down the wrong path. He means that desiring money causes people to stop having faith.
Here, the word faith could refer to: (1) the act of having faith in Jesus; (2) what people believe about Jesus when they have faith in him.
Paul speaks about people who cause grief for themselves as if they were using a sword to stab themselves. He means that they are responsible for the many sorrows that they experience.
6:11: Paul speaks of these temptations and sins as if they were things a person could physically run away from. He means that Timothy should always avoid these things.

Paul speaks of righteousness and other good qualities as if they were things that a person could run after and catch. He means that Timothy should try very hard to be characterized by these good things.
6:12: ἀγωνίζου τὸν καλὸν ἀγῶνα τῆς πίστεως

Here, Paul speaks about how Timothy should persevere in believing in and obeying Jesus as if he were a warrior fighting at his best or an athlete doing his best to win an event. He means that Timothy will encounter opposition, pain, and problems, but he should persist and persevere in believing in and obeying Jesus.
Here, the phrase the good fight could indicate: (1) that someone is fighting well; (2) that the fight is right or just.

Here Paul tells Timothy to desire and focus on eternal life so much that it is like holding onto it firmly with his hands. Paul may be continuing the metaphor of an athlete who worked hard to win an event and now holds the trophy in his hands.

Here, the phrase the good confession refers to what Christians would say when they publicly declared that they were Christians. Most likely, they confessed that they considered Jesus to be Lord and that they believed in him.
Here Paul implies that Timothy’s confession of his faith was binding because these witnesses were present and could testify that he had made it.
6:13: Here Paul puts Timothy under oath; he makes him swear by God and Christ Jesus when he gives him a command.
τοῦ μαρτυρήσαντος ἐπὶ Ποντίου Πειλάτου τὴν καλὴν ὁμολογίαν
Here Paul refers to what happened when Jesus was on trial before the Roman governor, Pontius Pilate. When Pilate asked Jesus who he was, Jesus told the truth even though it was dangerous to do so.
6:14: τηρῆσαί σε τὴν ἐντολὴν ἄσπιλον ἀνεπίλημπτον

Here, the adjectives spotless and irreproachable could modify: (1) you. In this case, Timothy should be spotless and irreproachable as he keeps the commandment; (2) the commandment. In this case, Timothy is supposed preserve the commandment that he obeys and teaches so that it remains spotless and irreproachable.
The terms spotless and irreproachable mean similar things. Paul is using the two terms together for emphasis.
Here Paul speaks as if he wants Timothy to be physically clean, without any spots or defects. He means that Timothy should not commit any sins or do anything wrong.
6:15: Here, the phrase translated in its own times indicates that Jesus’ appearance will happen at an appropriate time or period of time. More specifically, the times could be appropriate because: (1) they fit with Jesus’ appearance; (2) God chose them.
Here Paul means that God is the only Sovereign over whom no one else rules. He does not mean that no one else rules.
ὁ Βασιλεὺς τῶν βασιλευόντων, καὶ Κύριος τῶν κυριευόντων
The phrases King of the ones reigning and Lord of the ones ruling mean similar things. Paul is using the two phrases together for emphasis.
6:16: Here Paul means that God is the only One who always has and always will exist. He will never die or cease to exist. While Christians believe that those who trust in Jesus will live forever, God is the one who enables them to do that. So, God is the only one who lives forever without the help of someone else’s power.
Here Paul describes the light that fills God’s dwelling place in heaven. No one can come near this place because of how bright that light is.
Here, the word translated as eternal could describe: (1) power; (2) how God has honor and power.
6:17: Here, the phrase the present age refers to the time period in which Paul and Timothy lived, the time period before Jesus comes back and God transforms everything.
Paul says all here as an overstatement for emphasis.
6:18: The phrases to do good and to be rich in good works mean similar things. Paul is using the two phrases together for emphasis.
Here Paul speaks of good works as if they were money that could make people rich if they did many good works. He means that these believers should do very many good works.
The terms generous and willing to share mean similar things. Paul is using the two terms together for emphasis.
6:19: ἀποθησαυρίζοντας ἑαυτοῖς θεμέλιον καλὸν εἰς τὸ μέλλον

Here Paul speaks of doing the good works that he has just listed as if that were to be storing up treasure. He means that good things done in this life will ensure good things for life after Jesus comes back. Paul also speaks as if doing those good works would construct a good foundation. He means that people who do those good works will be certain to experience good things from the moment when Jesus comes back.

Here Paul is referring to the coming age, or time period. This coming age contrasts with “the present age” that Paul referred to in 6:17. The coming age is the time period after Jesus comes back and God transforms everything.
Here Paul speaks about believers gaining real life as if they were holding onto it firmly in their hands.
Many ancient manuscripts read the real life.
6:20: Here, the word deposit refers to something that has been entrusted to Timothy and that he must guard. This deposit could be: (1) the gospel, which God entrusted to Timothy; (2) the instructions Paul has given in this letter; (3) Timothy’s commission or ministry.
Here Paul implies that the sayings are empty of useful or true information.
Here, the word oppositions could refer to: (1) things that false teachers say to contradict and critique the gospel; (2) things that the false teachers say that are not consistent.
6:21: Paul speaks as if the faith were a mark or target that some people have missed. Paul means that these people have failed to continue in the faith.
Here, the word faith could refer to: (1) the act of having faith in Jesus; (2) what people believe about Jesus when they have faith in him.
As was customary in his culture, Paul closes his letter with a blessing for Timothy and the believers with him. He implies that the Grace is from God.
Many ancient manuscripts read you. Other ancient manuscripts read “you.
